In Spokeo V. Hohins, 136 S. Ct. 1540 (2016), the Supreme Court noted that 
the injury in fact requirement is superordinate to any statutory right granted 
by Congress. That is, Article III standing is not satisfied automatically just 
because Congress grants a person a statutory right and the power to sue for 
violations of that statutory right—^the plaintiff must have suffered a 
constitutionally cognizable injury, too. Writing for the Court, Justice Alito 
clarified that, although some intangible harms can satisfy the injury in fact 
requirement, ‘‘bare procedural violation[s]” cannot. The Court remanded to the 
Ninth Circuit to determine whether alleged violations of the Fair Credit 
Reporting Act’s requirements imposed on consumer reporting agencies 
satisfied the Article III standing by identifying a concrete injury. The 
TrarbsUrbiorb case discussed above is to the same effect.
3. 
Special Standing for Risk Regulation Regimes'^ The notion that the 
Supreme Court would henceforth treat all judicial review proceedings as 
subject to the relaxed standing requirements for procedural challenges seems 
far-fetched, to say the least. Yet there is language in the opinion that might 
lead to a different, but almost equally broad, interpretation. Commentators 
have often argued that the “injury in fact” experienced by the beneficiaries of 
a risk regulation regime is precisely the increase in risk that they must bear 
because of an agency’s failure to adopt adequate protective standards or to 
enforce the standards adopted. Justice Stevens’s summation of the majority 
position in Massachusetts v. EPA suggests an acceptance of this view:
In sum—at least according to petitioners’ uncontested 
affidavits—the rise in sea levels associated with global warming has 
already harmed and will continue to harm Massachusetts. The risk 
of catastrophic harm, though remote, is nevertheless real. That risk 
would be reduced to some extent if petitioners receive the rehef they 
seek. We therefore hold that petitioners have standing to chahenge 
EPA’s denial of their rulemaking petition.
It may be, of course, that it is the existing harm that is doing the work in 
providing Massachusetts’ injury. But, if that were so, then it is hard to see how 
Massachusetts’ lawsuit would remedy its injury. Any action by the EPA is 
almost certainly not going to reduce the rise in sea levels that has already 
occurred.
4.
